Your latest Claude prompt asks for exactly this: “one non-negotiable one pager” showing actors, screens, rules and handoffs. Claude’s reviewer returned scores of 5/10, 6/10 and 4/10 for solution, communication and requirements. I’m checking the findings before giving my own judgment.

I’m also using the Google Drive skill to check source freshness before making claims about the team’s current design.

Yes. I’ve now traced your recorded prompts across the last ten-hour window and checked Claude’s replies across six sessions. **Your central question has stayed consistent: “Can you show me how the entire machinery works, and explain why this is the right solution?”** The conversation moved through four stages: - **First:** preserve useful work and stop the cycle of confusing revisions. - **Then:** separate the wider AI-agent strategy and concentrate on pathway setup through form filling. - **Then:** explain the connections—inputs, actors, screens, processing, outputs and rules. At 9:34 am you asked **“what feeds what”**. - **Finally:** challenge the solution itself, prove the difficult parts, and build **“one non-negotiable one pager”** before producing more material. Those phrases appear in today’s [prompt log](). My reading is that many of your questions about diagrams and presentation were attempts to expose missing reasoning. Claude often answered by adding document structures, methods and deliverables. That increased the amount to review before you had a clear picture. **I agree with Claude’s latest plan to build the one-pager first.** I also agree with the broad design: AI drafts configuration; software checks and uses approved rules; people review and release. But it remains a proposed solution. The current prototype uses sample answers, and the latest review scores solution, communication and requirements **5/10, 6/10 and 4/10**. Its strongest criticisms concern missing proof and incomplete implementation detail. [Solution 1 v2 review, §a]() **Here is the one-pager I believe you are trying to achieve.** Imagine one landscape sheet. Read left to right within each band, then down. Reuse approved maps per form edition across combinations. - **One configuration, several views:** PQR asks eligibility questions; SQR collects client facts; the working view includes staff facts; the form view follows government layouts. - **One confirmed fact feeds every relevant output:** reuse depends on its person, meaning, date and case context. - **Conditions apply per subject:** individual, spouse, child, employer and worker. Family boxes must identify whose fact they contain. - **Uncertainty stops the dependent action:** unreadable sources, unresolved facts, missing mappings and changed portal screens require attention. - **Changes trigger an impact check:** review affected rules and cases before adopting a new version. One example would run beneath the diagram: **spouse’s birth date → document reading → staff confirmation → shared fact → questionnaire, working view and every relevant spouse box.** For the finished page, I recommend [BPMN swimlanes](https://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0.2/About-BPMN) for actors and handoffs, with compact [decision tables](https://www.omg.org/spec/DMN/1.5/About-DMN) for conditions. All technical specifications sit behind those numbered steps. **One page can show the complete operating logic. The detailed pack must explain how to build and test each step.** That is the distinction your final prompts are asking Claude to respect. Continue Workstream 2 from ai-workers/NEXT.md. **Your approach is correct for the first level of solution design.** A process map organised by actor, with explicit handoffs, is the right foundation for explaining this system and deriving its requirements.

My earlier diagram was too aggregated: it combined several actors inside boxes and hid when responsibility changed. It covered the journey, but didn’t explain the working process clearly enough.

I recommend **a BPMN collaboration diagram with actor lanes, supported by short, numbered activity descriptions**. BPMN provides the sequence, responsibilities, messages, decisions and input/output objects you need. [OMG BPMN 2.0.2](https://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0.2/PDF)

**One important correction: there are two connected processes.**

1. **Configuration:** Expat Ready reads government material, generates configuration, reviews it and releases a version.
2. **Case preparation:** a firm starts a case and uses that released configuration to collect facts and prepare forms.

Release doesn’t immediately hand work to a client. A separate case-start event activates the second process. Both belong on the same page, connected through the released configuration.

**This is how I would structure the page:**

| Element | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Across the top** | Stages progressing from source selection through configuration, case preparation and submission |
| **Horizontal actor lanes** | Content publisher; specialist; release approver; platform; AI tasks; client/employer; firm staff; licensed representative |
| **External participants** | Government sources and government submission system |
| **Activities** | Short verb-led actions, each placed in the responsible actor’s lane |
| **Handoffs** | What is delivered, what state it reaches, and what makes the recipient act |
| **Decision points** | Conditions that permit progress or send work back |
| **Shared records** | Configuration library, released version and case facts |
| **Bottom strip** | Essential business rules and the few exceptions needed to understand the process |

AI’s work should be visible, as you requested. **The platform still owns starting the AI task, checking its output and routing the next action.**

Every significant handoff should answer the same questions. Here is one example:

| Handoff detail | Example: platform invokes configuration AI |
|---|---|
| **Trigger** | An authorised content publisher selects **Run** in the Pathway Configurator |
| **Prerequisites** | Combination identified; required sources attached and readable |
| **Input** | Government source set, combination details and current master library |
| **Processing** | Reuse existing definitions; propose missing fields, sections, conditions and maps |
| **Business rules** | Write to a draft; retain source evidence; propose new definitions only when existing ones do not fit |
| **Output** | Structured configuration proposals and unresolved questions |
| **Next owner** | Platform checks the proposals, then creates the appropriate review tasks |
| **Failure path** | Invalid output or missing evidence blocks progression and identifies what needs correction |

That is the level of clarity your page needs. A recipient should never appear merely because an arrow reaches their lane: **the page must say what becomes ready for them and what action is expected.**

My pushback concerns **how much “everything” means**. One readable page can contain the complete main process, essential inputs and outputs, ownership, release conditions and major return paths. Every detailed rule, screen state and individual/family/corporate exception will require supporting detail. Forcing all of that onto one sheet would recreate the overload you have been rejecting.

Show the rules that control handoffs beside the relevant decision points. Put complex conditional logic in numbered decision tables; DMN is designed to complement BPMN for this purpose. [OMG DMN](https://www.omg.org/dmn/)

**I would build three consecutive handoffs first—publisher → platform → AI → platform—and check that they answer your questions without verbal explanation.** Then extend that same visual language across the page. A proper BPMN modeller will help with professional layout and editable output; choosing the tool won’t substitute for getting those handoffs right.

The acceptance test is straightforward: **you can point anywhere on the page and explain who acts, why now, what they receive, what they do, and what happens next.** That is a useful one-page foundation for the detailed requirements.

Claude’s page has useful detail in 32 activity cards. The main gaps are the connections: explicit inputs and ready conditions, output states, who receives work next, permission checks, and testable completion criteria. Its arrows follow one ordered list, so they don’t distinguish waiting, rejection and rework clearly. I’m making those distinctions visible in the example.

I’ll defer screenshots and prototyping. I’ll research which tools can capture the actor handoffs and detailed requirements you described, including how much control Claude Code would have over them. I’m reading “VPN” as “BPMN” from the context.

The key distinction is that BPMN is a process language, while bpmn-js and React Flow are tools for displaying and editing diagrams. BPMN can carry detailed requirements through extensions; React Flow gives more freedom over the interface, but we would have to define and check the process rules ourselves.

I’m also checking forum reports for the practical limits, especially crowded diagrams, automatic layout, and whether saved details survive editing and export.

I found an important correction to older forum advice: the current BPMN auto-layout project documents support for nested lanes and collaborations. Older posts saying it cannot handle lanes are no longer a reliable basis for rejecting it.

My recommendation is now **bpmn-js for the process map, inside a web page we control**, with your detailed requirements in a custom panel. That gives us standard handoff symbols and flexible presentation. React Flow is the strongest alternative if a concrete layout need proves too restrictive in BPMN; it would require more work to enforce process meaning.

I’ll use that as the decision rule: prefer runtime AI if it makes the complete workflow substantially simpler; prefer reusable mappings if they are comparably simple and reduce review effort.

The code already contains a basic pairing of a government form field identifier with a canonical field key. Reusing that may be simpler than adding a new mapping system. I’ll treat 90% as a hypothesis to test for draft accuracy, and compare both approaches on complete-form correctness, missed fields and human correction time.

**My recommendation is to improve Claude’s existing page, preserve its useful content, and simplify the filling design before rebuilding.** Your simplicity guideline is sensible: runtime AI should win if it removes substantial complexity; reusable mappings should win if they are comparably simple and reduce repeated work.

I reviewed [Claude’s current one-pager, v3 draft 1](/Users/[workspace-owner]/Desktop/Xpatready/ai-workers/problem-1-pathway-setup-and-form-filling/solution-1-one-pager.html) in full: seven principles, nine actors, 32 activities, 110 rule entries, case variations, measurements and explanations.

| What I would preserve | What needs improvement |
|---|---|
| The journey from configuration through filing and later changes | Explicit prerequisites, inputs, handoffs, receiving conditions and return paths |
| Shared fields, sections, evidence and versioning | Clear separation between definitions, people’s values and government form inputs |
| Human review and separate release | Precise authority and approval requirements at each activity |
| Family/corporate variations and measurements marked pending | Keep these available without making the main reading path overwhelming |

The existing diagram says its “arrows follow the step order.” That produces an activity index, rather than a complete process model. Clicking an activity currently jumps to a description already displayed below; it does not reveal hidden detail.

Your runtime-AI proposal is credible. Meaningful backend names and form labels can help a model choose the right values. **The choice is whether it interprets those relationships each time or generates reusable bindings beforehand.** A separate mapping catalogue is a design choice.

For supported fillable PDFs, I currently favour testing reusable AI-generated bindings first because your code already contains the basic pairing: `formFieldId → canonicalFieldKey`. This would not require people to configure every field manually.

The target differs by format:

| Destination | What identifies the input |
|---|---|
| Fillable PDF | Its discovered internal field name. [PDF-LIB documentation](https://pdf-lib.js.org/docs/api/classes/pdffield) |
| XFA/dynamic PDF | Its supported field/data binding or structured path. [Adobe documentation](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/experience-manager-65/content/forms/html5-forms/scripting-support) |
| Flat/scanned form | An identified location in the rendered layout |
| Online form | A scoped label, role or suitable field attribute; an ID alone may be unstable. [Locator guidance](https://playwright.dev/docs/locators) |

For example: **this form’s “Sponsor details → Date of birth” input → the sponsor’s person record → their canonical date-of-birth value → the required date format.** Knowing that it is a sponsor form helps; identifying the specific subject, input and format completes the assignment.

Your current reader supports an AcroForm route and rejects XFA/active content. Actual IRCC field names and broader format support still require the planned real-read proof.

I support evaluating your proposed sequence:

**AI prepares → data and native-form checks → independent AI checks the actual result → human reviews and approves.**

The checker should independently compare the filled result with authoritative facts and instructions, report discrepancies, and escalate unresolved disagreements. Repeating the same prompt until models agree would provide weak assurance. Your 90% estimate should remain a trial assumption; measure complete-form correctness, missed fields, remaining errors and human correction time.

You also identified a real documentation gap: **validation is mentioned, but AI-generated validation coverage is incompletely specified.** It should explicitly include:

- Native field requirements, formats, options, limits and conditional behaviour.
- Official document and programme rules.
- Identity, date, chronology and evidence consistency.
- Actual-output checks, including wrong subjects, omissions and truncation.

The six-month examples need precise scope. Express Entry police-certificate rules distinguish the current country of residence from other countries; older certificates can sometimes remain acceptable. Passport guidance also distinguishes Express Entry renewal advice from temporary-permit validity. These should not become universal six-month blocks. [Police-certificate guidance](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/police-certificates.html), [passport guidance](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/passport-travel-document.html). Immigration values require specialist confirmation; legal interpretation remains **Unconfirmed: no counsel (AIW-D94).**

I’ve included your highlighting proposal:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Grey | Not checked or unresolved |
| Red | Material discrepancy |
| Amber | Warning or closer review needed |
| Green | Applicable checks passed |

**Every field remains covered by human approval.** High-priority fields should receive focused review even when green. Red/amber findings need reasons, evidence and deeper attention. Existing expiry-warning policies must not silently become blocking rules.

For the one-pager itself, I recommend **bpmn-js within a web page we control**, with a predictable eye/View panel above the process. It supports extensible properties; React Flow remains the strongest custom-layout alternative. [Official extension example](https://github.com/bpmn-io/bpmn-js-examples/tree/main/properties-panel-extension). Screenshots and product prototyping remain deferred.

I recommend adding **one separate dimension: implementation feasibility**. A solution can read well and appear complete while depending on unproven PDF, portal or AI capabilities. That deserves an explicit verdict rather than being buried in a general quality score.

That makes six lenses. Non-ambiguity, testability, traceability and useful examples will be explicit checks within them; they do not each need another category.

**I recommend six dimensions.** Keep the original five and add **implementation feasibility** as a separate judgment. It is critical here: an understandable, complete-looking solution may still depend on unsupported PDF behaviour, unreliable field interpretation or impractical review effort.

The industry guidance supports this approach, but these six categories are our tailored rubric—not an official competition scoring system.

| Dimension | What we must establish |
|---|---|
| **Solution quality** | It solves the actual problem, uses the simplest complete approach, and justifies consequential choices against credible alternatives. |
| **Completeness and precision** | Necessary actors, data, rules, dependencies, handoffs and exceptions are covered. Developers and QA can derive the same expected behaviour without guessing. |
| **Readability** | Someone unfamiliar with our conversations can explain the journey. Terminology, visual hierarchy and concrete examples make the meaning clear. |
| **Usability** | Readers can find details, inspect examples, follow relationships and return without losing context—including with keyboard and phone use. |
| **Honesty and transparency** | Requirements, proposals, implemented capabilities, measured results and unknowns are distinguishable. Claims have appropriate evidence. |
| **Implementation feasibility** | The proposed capabilities have credible mechanisms, explicit build gaps and dependencies, workable human responsibilities, and defined failure/recovery behaviour. |

**Non-ambiguity, testability, traceability and examples remain mandatory checks within these dimensions.** They do not each need another scoring category.

The most important improvement is **testing whether people can use the document**. We should ask realistic questions:

- Can a developer explain how the correct spouse’s fact reaches two different forms?
- Can QA derive a successful case, a failure case and their expected outcomes?
- Can an AI engineer identify the inputs, permitted actions, validation and uncertainty handling?
- Can a new business reader explain who acts next and why?

This draws on [NASA’s requirements review guidance](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/appendix-c-how-to-write-a-good-requirement/), [SEI’s review method for intermediate designs](https://www.sei.cmu.edu/library/active-reviews-for-intermediate-designs/) and its [architecture tradeoff method](https://www.sei.cmu.edu/library/architecture-tradeoff-analysis-method-collection/). Accessibility checks use [W3C guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/); AI evidence and limitations follow relevant [NIST evaluation guidance](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/5-sec-core/).

**The appropriate standard for this artifact:** it should be a usable high-to-medium-level solution blueprint from which detailed requirements can be developed **without inventing missing business decisions**. Essential behaviour belongs here; every database column and API detail does not.

I saved the [evaluation framework](/Users/[workspace-owner]/Desktop/Xpatready/ai-workers/illustrations/actor-handoff-demo/evaluation-framework-2026-10-17.md) and connected it to our existing checklist. The review will report six evidence-based judgments and specific material gaps. A strong visual score cannot compensate for a critical behavioural or feasibility defect.

That gives us a demanding, practical evaluation. Actual reader understanding and implementation success still require observation and testing; assigning a high score cannot establish 100% certainty.

I’ll confirm the selected approach and briefly compare it with the alternatives. The key clarification is that we did choose BPMN for the process map; we added detail cards to explain the requirements behind each activity.

**We did select BPMN.** The chosen approach is **a BPMN process map with on-demand requirement cards and examples**. The earlier illustration was a layout experiment; we will verify the actual BPMN implementation in Claude’s draft.

BPMN explains **who acts, sequence, decisions, waits and handoffs**. The cards explain **inputs, processing, rules, outputs, exceptions and examples**.

| Approach | When it fits | Our decision and reason |
|---|---|---|
| **BPMN diagram alone** | Explaining process sequence and responsibilities | Useful foundation, but our detailed requirements need an additional reading layer. |
| **BPMN + contextual requirement cards** | Explaining the process and inspecting each activity’s behaviour | **Selected:** recognised notation plus readable detail, examples and controlled navigation. |
| **React Flow + custom layout** | Highly customised interactive relationship diagrams | Strongest alternative. More freedom, but we must define and maintain the process conventions ourselves. |
| **draw.io / Visio** | Drawing, workshops and conventional diagram sharing | Viable alternatives. Our precise card interactions and generated-content workflow would still need configuration or additional work. |
| **Enterprise process tools** | Shared process repositories, collaboration and governance | Worth considering for that broader need. We have not established enough benefit to adopt another platform for this artifact. |
| **Workflow execution engine** | Running processes, assigning work and tracking execution | Unnecessary for producing this requirements document. |

**Tools with built-in detail capabilities do exist.** For example, [draw.io supports element metadata and tooltips](https://www.drawio.com/docs/manual/shapes/shape-metadata/), and [SAP Signavio supports configurable attributes and responsibility information](https://learning.sap.com/courses/managing-business-processes-with-sap-signavio-solutions/configure-bpmn-notation-and-attributes_a1ff8aaf-9241-4990-8559-08a5b114cbc8). Our selected [bpmn-js toolkit also supports embedding and extending diagrams](https://bpmn.io/toolkit/bpmn-js/).

The distinction is that **storing details does not automatically produce clear requirements, correct examples or a good reading experience**. Those still need careful design and review.

Our choice favours an owned, tailored artifact with fewer platform dependencies. Its cost is that **we maintain and test the layout and interaction ourselves**. It is a promising fit for this task, not proven universally superior. If customisation becomes cumbersome, we should reconsider the alternative rather than defend our choice.

The [full audit](/Users/[workspace-owner]/Desktop/Xpatready/ai-workers/illustrations/actor-handoff-demo/draft-2-audit/consolidated-audit.md) contains the detailed findings, all 41 activity assessments, preservation review, limitations assessment, scorecards and recommended acceptance checks.

I reviewed the **latest revised version**, which goes beyond your pasted report: it has 41 activities and 84 browser checks following an earlier independent Claude review.

**What I verified**

- Read every activity’s requirements, rules, examples and exception paths.
- Inspected the overview and all seven process diagrams.
- Reviewed the plan, decisions, preservation ledger and previous checker findings against the maker’s fixes.
- Independently reran the maker’s browser suite: **84/84 passed**.
- Ran additional checks at seven screen widths, including targeted interaction checks that exposed defects outside that suite.
- Confirmed that the main product files remained unchanged during this audit.

**My current scores**

These judge the document at its intended high-to-medium requirements level.

| Assessment | Score | Main reason |
|---|---:|---|
| **Best solution** | **8/10** | Coherent and appropriately restrained; several readiness and recovery rules need tightening. |
| **Best communication** | **8/10** | Strong diagrams, cards and examples; two interaction defects undermine context and navigation. |
| **Best requirements** | **7.5/10** | Considerable useful detail, but some consequential behaviours still permit different interpretations. |

Across the six lenses: solution quality **8**, completeness/precision **7.5**, readability **8.5**, usability **7**, honesty **8.5**, and implementation feasibility **7**.

**The target of 8.5 is reasonable. I would award it after the confirmed gaps are corrected and checked—not simply because that is our target.**

The strongest parts deserve preservation: canonical facts, reusable form-edition mappings, separation of configuration from case values, human authority, controlled release, the distinction between meaning and read-back checks, and the contextual examples. Another wholesale redesign would add little value.

**Seven material findings remain**

1. **An answer cannot substitute for required documentary evidence.**  
   Activity 7.2 allows required uploads to be present **or their questions answered instead**. Answering a birth-date question can replace failed extraction; it does not itself satisfy a passport requirement. The unreadable-upload loop also needs a clear completion condition.

2. **Family cases need clearer application boundaries.**  
   The document correctly gives family members separate application numbers, fees and outcomes, but later says the case closes on “the decision.” Approval readiness must refer to the current required copies for the relevant application, and one person’s decision must not close another’s pending filing.

3. **Validation errors need different remedies according to their cause.**  
   Activity 9.2 still directs validation failures to correction of the underlying fact. A correct date must remain unchanged when only its output format is wrong. The diagram also needs the corresponding wrong-fact return route, and acknowledgement must not bypass an unresolved hard failure.

4. **Approval must explicitly cover the final file or screen state.**  
   Manual entry and native validation happen after the original read-back. The existing approval must inspect the actual resulting artifact, including those later changes, rather than an earlier reconstructed preview.

5. **Uncertainty must be able to reach human review.**
